children: Oil rose Tuesday as renewed tensions in the Middle East kept fears of supply disruptions elevated.

The recent exchange of attacks between the U.S. and Iran prompted President Trump to say the U.S. would "hit them hard." American forces said they had hit Iranian launch sites that were preparing to fire rockets used to deploy naval mines in the Strait of Hormuz. In return, Tehran fired a salvo of missiles at Jordan, which is home to thousands of American troops. All were intercepted.

"The main theme was the renewed escalation in the U.S.-Iran conflict," Commerzbank Research analysts said in a note. "The renewed hostilities dashed recent hopes of progress toward normalizing shipping through the strait," the analysts said. Trump "also signaled that Washington was prepared to conduct further attacks," the analysts added.
Front-month West Texas Intermediate crude oil futures rose 1.0% to $86.60 per barrel and front-month Brent crude oil futures added 0.7% to $91.16 a barrel, according to ICE data.
Meanwhile, equity markets across Asia-Pacific were mostly lower, as higher oil prices fueled concerns over inflation.
Japan's Nikkei Stock Average declined 0.3%, Malaysia's FTSE Bursa Malaysia KLCI shed 0.5% and Singapore's FTSE Straits Times Index lost 0.2%. Meanwhile, South Korea's Kospi edged 0.2% higher.

"Oil prices jumped with Brent oil climbing back above $90 [per barrel], reviving inflation concerns and spilling into" equities and government bonds, said Rodrigo Catril, senior FX strategist at National Australia Bank, in commentary.

The yield on Japan's 10-year government bonds rose 3 basis points to 2.970%, the highest intraday level since September 1996. Yields on Australia's 10-year sovereign debt climbed 8 basis points to 5.1430% and those on New Zealand's 10-year government securities rose 6 basis points to 4.7940%. Bond yields move inversely to prices.
